page.title: A tiny physics lab
page.description: A tiny physics bench. Predict, change one thing, and see what happens. Then try three questions without the controls.

props.text: Your turn: leave the controls alone for these three questions. Each uses the same ideal spring model, at rest, with gravity 9.8 m/s².

questions.question: Double the mass on the same spring. What happens to its extension at rest?
questions.explanation: Doubling mass doubles weight. With stiffness unchanged, x = mg/k doubles too. Try 0.5 kg, then 1 kg; compare the extension, not the spring's total length.

questions.question: Keep the mass at 1 kg, but double the stiffness. What happens to the spring's upward force at rest?
questions.explanation: At rest, the upward force must still balance the same 9.8 N weight. A stiffer spring produces that force with less extension, not a larger force at equilibrium. Keep mass fixed and compare two stiffnesses.

questions.question: A 0.5 kg mass hangs from a 200 N/m spring. How much does it extend?
questions.explanation: Weight = 0.5 × 9.8 = 4.9 N. Extension = 4.9 ÷ 200 = 0.0245 m = 2.45 cm. The 4.9 is a force in newtons, not a length in centimetres. Check the units before using the controls.

items.text: Predict what happens if mass and stiffness both double
Test 0.5 kg / 100 N/m, then 1 kg / 200 N/m
Explain why the extension is unchanged

props.label: Show the reasoning
props.text: At equilibrium, spring force kx balances weight mg, so x = mg/k. Doubling both mass and stiffness leaves their ratio unchanged. Extension is measured from the unloaded length. This ideal model omits the spring's own weight, oscillation and elastic limits.

reply: A ready-made spring experiment, not a generated simulation. Change the mass or stiffness, compare the extension, then try the three-question check. The controls and quiz work without a model; preview progress is temporary.
